messages.text: based on the work you've done in "C:\Users\k\Repository\Veehiicuul2" and "C:\Users\k\Repository\Win32_DemoApp", i think win32 gui controls may not be the right direction for veehiicuul. i want you to rewrite veehiicuul using the "Custom GPU-rendered UI" approach you described earlier in C:\Users\k\Repository\Veehiicuul3.

I’ll build Veehiicuul3 as a separate C++/DirectX 12 project with a custom GPU-rendered interface, carrying forward the modeler, track builder and driving workflows. I’ll preserve Veehiicuul2 and Win32_DemoApp, and keep on-demand rendering for idle editor views.
one reason i want this is to avoid framework "baggage" that win32 gui or other frameworks bring.

I’ll keep the UI layer small and purpose-built, without substituting another general-purpose widget framework. Windows will still provide the window, input and platform services; we’ll control the in-app layout, drawing and interaction. That also means we’ll own details such as text editing, keyboard navigation and accessibility.
these ui frameworks bring a tremendous amount of "batteries included" functionality, but the cost of that added complexity may outweigh the benefits they bring

That’s the tradeoff: useful built-in behavior can come with assumptions and machinery that don’t fit your workflow. For Veehiicuul3, I’ll build only the controls it needs, with shared behavior so we don’t recreate the sidebar inconsistencies. Custom UI isn’t automatically faster or simpler, so I’ll measure idle rendering, responsiveness and resource use rather than assume the rewrite improves them.
for now, don't attempt to replicate the complete functionality of ui frameworks. instead, focus on minimal, barebones functionality

I’ll keep it barebones: just the controls needed for the current workflows, with simple drawing, clicking, scrolling and numeric editing. Broader framework features can wait until there’s a concrete need.
for example, don't try to implement "tab navigation" at all
Understood. No Tab-key navigation in Veehiicuul3.
don't worry about accessibility stuff
I’ll leave accessibility features out of scope for now.
also, ensure that you can continue development uninterrupted if i lock this machine

I’ll keep coding, building and running noninteractive tests while it’s locked, and continue other implementation work when a visual check has to wait. Locking won’t be a reason to stop development. The machine still needs to stay awake and connected; I won’t change its security or power settings.
to simplify things, the application only runs in 2560*1440 resolution borderless fullscreen window mode
also, as before, only use dx12

Veehiicuul3 will use DirectX 12 only, with a fixed 2560×1440 borderless-fullscreen layout. If the selected monitor’s desktop resolution differs, should it scale that fixed layout to fill the monitor, or require the monitor to be set to 2560×1440?
scale that fixed layout to fill the monitor

currently, the max resolution of the ne18nz2 monitor is 1920*1200. if you can only launch the app on ne18nz2, is it possible to properly render the app at 2560*1440 in borderless fullscreen window mode? or do you need a 2560*1440 monitor?

Yes. DX12 can render into a 2560×1440 offscreen image, then scale it into a 1920×1200 borderless-fullscreen window on NE18NZ2. A 2560×1440 monitor isn’t required.

One tradeoff: 2560×1440 is 16:9, while 1920×1200 is 16:10. Filling the entire monitor stretches the image slightly, and downscaling loses some fine detail. We can test the full layout and mouse mapping there, but judging native-resolution sharpness requires a matching display or inspecting a full-resolution capture.

That follows your requested scale-to-fill behavior without changing the monitor’s resolution.
what if NE18NZ2 had 3840x2400 resolution? would you be able to properly launch and test the app at 2560x1440 borderless fullscreen window mode?

Yes. The app would render at 2560×1440 internally, then upscale that image to fill a 3840×2400 borderless window.

That monitor is also 16:10, so filling it would stretch the 16:9 image: 1.5× horizontally and about 1.67× vertically. I could test fullscreen presentation, the UI and mouse mapping, but it wouldn’t be a pixel-for-pixel view of the original render.

The distinction is internal render resolution versus fullscreen window size. Borderless fullscreen uses the monitor’s desktop dimensions; our internal render stays 2560×1440.

Yes, if you mean displaying the app at exactly 2560×1440 pixels without scaling. We can make a borderless window covering the 3840×2400 display and place the unscaled app in the center, with black space around it. That preserves every rendered pixel and allows proper 1:1 testing.

The margins would be 640 pixels on each side and 480 pixels above and below. Should I use this unscaled, centered presentation instead of scaling to fill?
